extracted.intended_audience: USCIS asylum officers, EOIR immigration judges, DHS/DOJ rulewriters, immigration attorneys, and stakeholders affected by asylum/withholding rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory standards for applying/withdrawing the "Security Bars and Processing" rule: statutory bars to asylum/withholding, credible-fear/reasonable-possibility screening standards, public-health-based bars, procedures for AOs and Immigration Judges, and legal requirements for rulemaking and withdrawal. Includes interaction with intervening rulemakings and administrative-law constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory bars to asylum and withholding of removal
rubrics_metrics.description: The INA and implementing regulations impose mandatory bars to asylum eligibility (section 208(b)(2)(A)(i)-(v), 8 U.S.C. 1158(b)(2)(A)(i)-(v)) and to withholding of removal eligibility (section 241(b)(3)(B), 8 U.S.C. 1231(b)(3)(B)). These include persons who: (1) ordered, incited, assisted, or otherwise participated in persecution; (2) have been convicted of a particularly serious crime; (3) have serious reasons to believe they committed a serious nonpolitical crime outside the U.S.; (4) are reasonably believed to be a danger to the security of the U.S.; and (5) are described in certain terrorism-related provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text lists each statutory bar and cross-references the INA and CFR provisions. The preamble explains how these bars operate across asylum, statutory withholding, and CAT regulations and notes interplay with other statutory bars (e.g., deportability, genocide/torture involvement). Citations provided: INA sections and 8 CFR provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firm resettlement bar to asylum (separate sixth statutory bar)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sixth statutory bar applies only to asylum (not withholding): an alien who 'was firmly resettled in another country prior to arriving in the United States' is barred from asylum under INA 208(b)(2)(A)(vi), 8 U.S.C. 1158(b)(2)(A)(vi).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly distinguishes this bar from withholding bars and notes its different effect. The Departments note this bar is not applicable to withholding of removal eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and effect of 'particularly serious crime' and 'danger to the community' for withholding denial
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of section 241(b)(3)(B)(ii) (or earlier section 243(h)(2) formulations), an alien convicted of a particularly serious crime is considered to constitute a danger to the community, supporting mandatory denial of withholding. If evidence indicates applicability of grounds for denial, applicant bears burden to prove by a preponderance of the evidence that such grounds do not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble states the legal consequence (mandatory denial) and the allocation of burdens of proof. Cross-references to case law and regulatory provisions governing the 'particularly serious crime' determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credible fear screening standard: 'significant possibility' of eligibility for asylum
rubrics_metrics.description: In expedited removal, an alien has a 'credible fear of persecution' if 'there is a significant possibility, taking into account the credibility of the statements made by the alien ... and such other facts as are known to the officer, that the alien could establish eligibility for asylum.' INA 235(b)(1)(B)(v), 8 U.S.C. 1225(b)(1)(B)(v).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that the 'significant possibility' statutory standard asks whether the alien could establish eligibility for asylum (which itself requires a well-founded fear). The preamble contrasts this screening threshold with higher standards used elsewhere and cites Cardoza-Fonseca/Stevic.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Reasonable possibility' screening standard for withholding/CAT when bars operate
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an AO or Immigration Judge determines an alien does not have a significant possibility of eligibility for asylum due to the operation of a regulatory or statutory bar, the alien is screened for potential statutory withholding of removal and CAT protection under the 'reasonable possibility of persecution or torture' standard, a standard higher than the 'significant possibility' standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble explains this standard is about the possibility of harm occurring (not the ultimate eligibility standard) and is higher than the statutory credible fear threshold. Citations: Global Asylum Final Rule amendments and related CFR sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'More likely than not' standard for withholding/CAT decisions and certain screenings
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'more likely than not' (clear probability) standard applies to withholding of removal in full determinations (and in some screening contexts when an alien is subject to security bars): an alien is entitled to withholding if it is more likely than not that the alien would face persecution or torture in the country of removal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble cites INS v. Stevic and CFR provisions (e.g., 8 CFR 208.16, 1208.16) and explains when the 'more likely than not' standard is used in screening (e.g., when an alien might be able to establish asylum but is barred by security bars, the AO/Judge screens for torture on the 'more likely than not' standard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-health-emergency-based bar to withholding of removal
rubrics_metrics.description: If a communicable disease has triggered an ongoing federal public health emergency (e.g., under 42 U.S.C. 247d or 21 U.S.C. 360bbb-3), an alien is ineligible for withholding of removal under section 241(b)(3) and corresponding CAT regulations on the basis of being 'reasonable grounds for regarding the alien as a danger to the security of the United States' if the alien (A) exhibits symptoms indicating affliction with the disease per guidance issued by the Secretary/Attorney General; or (B) has come into contact with the disease within the number of days equivalent to the longest known incubation/contagion period per guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory text (8 CFR) and preamble specify the two alternative factual triggers (symptoms or recent contact within incubation period) and require relevant guidance from the Secretary or Attorney General. Explains linkage to declared federal public health emergencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger to public health caused by epidemic abroad (country-based designation)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Secretary and Attorney General, in consultation with HHS, jointly determine that aliens coming from (or who recently came from) specified foreign country(ies)/places where a communicable disease is prevalent would cause danger to U.S. public health, and designate the places and relevant time/circumstances, then aliens from those places who are still within the longest known incubation/contagion period may be regarded as a danger to U.S. security and be ineligible for withholding/CAT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies the interagency determination (Secretary + AG + consultation with HHS), the need to designate the foreign place(s) and period/circumstances, and that any relevant exceptions may be included. Ties to 42 CFR 34.2(b) definition of communicable disease of public health significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: AO/Immigration Judge procedures regarding application and timing of bars during credible-fear screening
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations require AOs and Immigration Judges, during credible fear screenings and reviews, to consider the applicability of any bars to applying for asylum or eligibility for asylum (including statutory/regulatory bars such as those in 8 CFR and INA sections cited). If an AO/Immigration Judge finds bars apply, they follow different screening standards and procedures (e.g., screen for withholding/CAT under different standards, possibly place in AWO proceedings, or refer to third-country removal as appropriate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble describes multiple concrete procedural consequences (consider bars during screening; shift to different screening thresholds; referral routes). It also notes that some intervening rules made consideration discretionary rather than mandatory and explains the conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretionary vs mandatory consideration of statutory bars during fear screenings
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS's later 'DHS Mandatory Bars Rule' allows AOs to consider statutory bars at their discretion (except the firm resettlement bar), whereas the Security Bars Final Rule would have made consideration of such bars mandatory in certain provisions (e.g., by adding paragraph (iv) to 8 CFR 208.30(e)(5)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble explains the practical differences: discretionary provisions let AOs decide whether to consider bars; the Security Bars Final Rule would have required application, creating inconsistency if both sets of text coexisted. Includes specific citations and compares screening standards that would apply under each approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screening standards vary by bar type and affect subsequent proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory text sets different screening standards depending on the applicable bar: current paragraph (ii) of 8 CFR 208.30(e)(5) provides that where alien 'appears to be subject' to mandatory bars other than firm resettlement, the AO 'may consider' those bars and the applicable screening standard for torture may be the 'significant possibility' standard; under the Security Bars Final Rule's proposed paragraph (iv), security bars would require screening for torture at the 'more likely than not' standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble highlights that having inconsistent provisions would change which screening standard applies (lower vs higher) for torture when mandatory bars are implicated and could create confusion; specific cross-references provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement into asylum-and-withholding-only (AWO) proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: If an alien meets the requisite burden on screening (e.g., shows credible fear or meets certain thresholds but is subject to bars), DHS may place the alien in AWO proceedings instead of section 240 removal proceedings. AWO proceedings permit application only for asylum, statutory withholding of removal, and CAT protection (see 8 CFR 1208.2(c)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains distinction between AWO and section 240 proceedings (AWO limits relief types). Preamble notes when DHS would place an alien in AWO (e.g., if meets burden but barred) and the regulatory text that establishes this procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-country removal and TCT (third-country transit) bar procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Security Bars Final Rule included provisions for third-country removals where aliens were ineligible for asylum due to the TCT Bar; intervening rulemakings (e.g., Lawful Pathways Final Rule) rescinded the TCT bar and removed the regulatory provisions. If Security Bars amendatory instructions 4 and 12 were not withdrawn, they would reinstate provisions governing TCT removal procedures that no longer exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble justifies withdrawing amendatory instructions to avoid codifying obsolete language and describes the interplay with the rescission of the TCT Bar Final Rule. Cross-references to specific regulatory paragraphs that would be affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting an alien's refusal to indicate desire for IJ review as declining review
rubrics_metrics.description: The Global Asylum Final Rule and Security Bars Final Rule provided that if an alien refused to indicate whether they want Immigration Judge review of a negative determination, DHS would consider such a refusal as declining review (i.e., declining IJ review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble notes which rule contained this provision and that intervening rules reversed this requirement; explains practical effect on review rights and screening process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of conflicting or confusing regulatory text when intervening rulemakings exist
rubrics_metrics.description: The Departments will withdraw amendatory instructions from the Security Bars Final Rule when those amendments would conflict with later- issued intervening rules or otherwise create confusing or obsolete regulatory text. Withdrawal is used to avoid overwriting intervening amendments without APA procedures and to preserve the status quo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble explains rationale: implementation without change would overwrite later amendments, create conflict, and risk confusing terminology and infeasible implementation. Withdrawal avoids unjustified reversion and respects APA procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative Procedure Act (APA): notice-and-comment requirement for substantive changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantive regulatory changes generally require notice-and-comment rulemaking under the APA. The Departments note they did not seek comments on modifying/rescinding the Security Bars Final Rule's substance in the delay IFRs and that rescission or modification would typically require notice-and-comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble discusses APA constraints (notice-and-comment), references to prior delay IFRs that solicited limited comment on effective date but not substance, and explains why wholesale reinstatement without APA compliance would be problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA: classification as procedural rule, good cause, and foreign-affairs exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory changes may be evaluated for whether they are a procedural rule (potentially exempt from notice-and-comment) or whether a 'good cause' or 'foreign affairs' exception to notice-and-comment applies. The Departments analyze these doctrines when justifying timing/effective-date and other procedural aspects of their rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble section on APA discusses these doctrines, explains when they might apply, and sets out that the Departments considered them in delaying and in withdrawing amendatory instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order regulatory-review obligations (EO 12866, EO 13563, EO 14192)
rubrics_metrics.description: Significant regulatory actions must satisfy Executive Order requirements for regulatory planning and review: e.g., analysis of costs/benefits, regulatory planning (EO 12866), improvements to retrospective review and regulatory quality (EO 13563), and EO 14192 deregulatory considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble lists the EOs considered and states the Departments' obligations to conduct required analyses and review through OMB as applicable; used in the Departments' evaluation of impacts and reasonableness of delay/withdrawal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) assessment requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must analyze rule impacts on small entities under the RFA and consider alternatives if significant economic impacts on a substantial number of small entities would occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble indicates RFA analysis was part of the statutory and regulatory requirements considered when finalizing the partial withdrawal and corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (UMRA) obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must analyze whether a rule includes mandates that result in expenditures by state, local, or tribal governments or the private sector above statutory thresholds and prepare appropriate statements/analyses under UMRA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble lists UMRA among the statutes considered in the rulemaking analysis and explains the Departments reviewed potential impacts consistent with UMRA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional Review Act (CRA) considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Final rulemakings must comply with CRA requirements (e.g., submission to Congress and determination whether a rule is 'major') and may trigger congressional disapproval procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble includes CRA among the statutory/regulatory requirements reviewed and notes whether the Departments treated the action accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federalism, tribal consultation, and civil justice reform considerations (EO 13132, EO 13175, EO 12988)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must consider federalism impacts (EO 13132), consult/coordinate with Indian tribal governments as appropriate (EO 13175), and ensure rules conform to civil justice reform principles (EO 12988).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble enumerates these executive orders and summarizes departmental consideration of their requirements in the rulemaking and withdrawal determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must consider environmental impacts and NEPA obligations when issuing rules and have instruction manuals/appendices to implement NEPA compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble refers to DHS's NEPA Instruction Manual and indicates NEPA obligations were considered; notes where copies are available and cross-references to the Instruction Manual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) — information collection review
rubrics_metrics.description: If the rule creates or amends collections of information, agencies must comply with PRA requirements (OMB approval, information-collection package).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble lists the PRA among statutes considered and indicates the Departments reviewed whether any PRA-covered information collections were affected by the partial withdrawal/corrections.
